nameStory: Devil's Beggarticks gets its devilish name from its incredibly annoying seeds that grab onto your clothes with tiny barbed hooks, clinging like desperate beggars. The "devil's" part comes from how frustrating these hitchhiking seeds are to remove - they seem designed by the devil himself to torment hikers and dog walkers! Other colorful names like "devil's pitchfork" and "sticktights" all refer to those same grabby, two-pronged seeds.
description: Devil's Beggarticks is a weedy annual herb that grows 1-4 feet tall in disturbed, moist areas throughout New England. It produces small, unremarkable yellow flowers that lack the showy petals of most sunflower family members, looking more like tiny yellow buttons. The plant is most notorious for its seeds, which are flat, brown, wedge-shaped hitchhikers armed with two barbed prongs that grab onto fur, feathers, and fabric. You'll often notice this plant more by its seeds stuck to your socks than by its modest flowers.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, brown, wedge-shaped seeds with two barbed prongs that feel rough and hook-like when you try to pull them off clothing - they're incredibly persistent and grabby

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flower heads about 1/4 inch across that lack the typical daisy petals - just tiny yellow disc flowers that look like miniature buttons

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves divided into 3-5 leaflets with toothed edges that feel slightly rough and papery when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branching annual herb 1-4 feet tall with a somewhat scraggly, weedy appearance and square-ish stems that feel rigid when bent

habitat: Look for Devil's Beggarticks in disturbed, moist soils like garden edges, ditches, stream banks, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in spots where the soil has been turned over or disturbed, often appearing along trails, roadsides, and the muddy edges of ponds. This opportunistic plant loves nutrient-rich, damp ground and partial sun.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small seedlings with their characteristic three-part leaves, often in disturbed soil from the previous year's seed bank.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin producing their small yellow buttonlike flowers from mid to late summer, though the blooms are easily overlooked.
seasonality.fall: The notorious barbed seeds mature and become prime hitchhiking season - this is when you'll most likely encounter the plant by finding seeds stuck to your clothes or pet's fur.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stems may persist with some seeds still attached, but most identification happens through seeds already dispersed and stuck to fabric.

funFact: A single Devil's Beggarticks plant can produce over 5,000 barbed seeds, and each seed can stick so tenaciously to fabric that indigenous peoples and early settlers actually used them as natural Velcro to attach feathers to arrows and repair torn clothing!
confusionNotes: Devil's Beggarticks is most easily confused with other beggarticks species, but its three-part leaves and distinctive two-pronged barbed seeds set it apart from most relatives. Remember: if it's grabbing your socks with flat, two-pronged hitchhikers, it's likely Devil's Beggarticks rather than the round, multi-barbed seeds of burdock or the single-pronged seeds of other plants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "devil's" this and "devil's" that, this native plant actually provides valuable late-season food for birds and pollinators when little else is blooming. The "beggarticks" name is shared by many Bidens species, all referring to their hitchhiking lifestyle of "begging" rides on passing animals.
compareHints: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower). Its seeds have exactly two barbed prongs, while some relatives have three or four prongs, and its flowers are consistently small yellow buttons without the variable petal displays of showier cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
